'''James Joseph Collins''' (born June 26, 1965) is an American [[bioengineer]] and [[biophysicist]] who is one of the founders of [[synthetic biology]]. He is known for pioneering synthetic [[gene networks]] and programmable cells, which launched the field of synthetic biology and influenced research in the detection and treatment of [[Ebola]], [[Zika virus|Zika]], and [[COVID-19]]. He pioneered the use of [[artificial intelligence]] in antibiotic discovery, identifying novel [[antibiotics]] effective against drug-resistant bacterial pathogens. He is also known for pioneering [[stochastic resonance]], [[neurostimulation]], and biological dynamics in the research of physiological and biological systems. He is the Termeer Professor of Medical Engineering & Science at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT).

After graduating from the [[College of the Holy Cross]], Collins earned his doctorate in medical engineering from the [[University of Oxford]] in 1990 as a [[Rhodes Scholar]]. He was a professor of biomedical engineering, a professor of medicine, University Professor, and the William Fairfield Warren Distinguished Professor at [[Boston University]], where he co-founded the Center for BioDynamics before moving to MIT in 2014. He is currently a director of the [[MIT Jameel Clinic]], a member of the [[Harvard–MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology]] and the [[Broad Institute]], and a core faculty member of the [[Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering|Wyss Institute]] at [[Harvard University]] and [[Institute for Medical Engineering and Science|IMES]].

Collins is an elected member of the [[National Academy of Medicine]], the [[National Academy of Engineering]], and the [[National Academy of Sciences]]. He was awarded a [[MacArthur Fellowship]] in 2003 for [[biotechnology]] research, the [[Lagrange Prize]] in 2010 for outstanding contributions to [[complexity science]], and the [[Dickson Prize in Medicine]] in 2020 for pioneering synthetic biology. He received the [[Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology]] in 2023 and was named a [[List of Clarivate Citation laureates in Chemistry|Clarivate Citation Laureate in Chemistry]] that same year for pioneering synthetic gene circuits.

== Early life and education<!--Note: Some of these citations apply also to other sentences in their respective section, especially preceding ones.--> ==
Collins was born on June 26, 1965, in the [[The Bronx|Bronx]], then moved to [[Bellerose, New York]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Khan |first=Firdos Alam |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J51_AwAAQBAJ&dq=James+Collins+%22June+26,+1965%22&pg=PA279 |title=Biotechnology in Medical Sciences |date=2014-05-08 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4822-2367-5 |language=en}}</ref> His father was an aviation engineer employed in [[NASA]] and military projects,<ref name=":0" /> and partly developed the optical system for the [[Apollo Lunar Module]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ellis |first=Danielle |date=2025-07-07 |title=Synthetic Biology and the Pursuit of Living Diagnostics and Therapeutics |url=https://www.news-medical.net/news/20250707/Synthetic-Biology-and-the-Pursuit-of-Living-Diagnostics.aspx |access-date=2026-05-25 |website=News-Medical |language=en|type=interview}}</ref> His mother was a mathematician.<ref name=":52">{{Citation |title=James Collins: Doing Good Science with an Underdog Spirit|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HB906zshzDw&t=105s|work=YouTube|publication-date=March 8, 2026|access-date=2023-08-13|series=|at=|publisher=Harvard Biotech Club|language=en|date=}}</ref> His paternal grandfather, Maurice Collins, and his paternal grandmother, Helen Kiely, were both Irish natives who were raised in [[Abbeyfeale]], [[County Limerick]], and [[Kiskeam]], [[County Cork]], respectively.<ref name=":2" /> At age 10, Collins moved to [[New Hampshire]] with his family after finishing elementary school,<ref>{{Cite web |title=From Dance Clubs to Syn Bio: MIT's Collins on Startups, Second Chances |url=https://aimbe.org/college-of-fellows/cof-0189/ |access-date=2023-12-19 |website=[[American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering]] |language=en |via=[[Xconomy]]}}</ref> growing up in [[Nashua, New Hampshire|Nashua]].<ref name="AC1914">{{Cite news |last=Baker |first=Billy |date=November 24, 2008 |title=Dream gig grants him freedom to explore |pages=16 |work=[[The Boston Globe]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/444360142/ |access-date=December 20, 2023}}</ref> He first developed an interest in medical engineering when one of his grandfathers became blind and the other suffered multiple strokes.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Trafton |first=Anne |date=2015-11-14 |title=Reprogramming biology: Biological engineer James Collins designs genetic circuits with novel functions |url=https://news.mit.edu/2015/profile-james-collins-1114 |access-date=2023-12-19 |website=[[MIT News]] |publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] |language=en}}</ref>

After high school, Collins initially intended to study electrical engineering in college. He was admitted to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), but chose instead to enroll at the [[College of the Holy Cross]] in [[Worcester, Massachusetts]], for the college's community.<ref name="biogInfo">{{Cite news |last=Reardon |first=Michael |author-link= |date=Winter 2007 |title=The Profile: James J. Collins Jr. '87 |volume=41 |pages=80 |newspaper=Holy Cross Magazine |publisher=[[College of the Holy Cross]] |issue=1 |url=http://www.holycross.edu/departments/publicaffairs/hcm/winter07/GAA/gaa8.html |url-status=dead |access-date=April 15, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160822154728/http://www.holycross.edu/departments/publicaffairs/hcm/winter07/GAA/gaa8.html |archive-date=August 22, 2016}}</ref> As an undergraduate at Holy Cross, he was a member of its track and [[Cross country running|cross country]] teams, and ran a 4:17 mile.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zaman |first=Muhammed |title=Biography of Resistance |date=2020-04-20 |publisher=Harper |isbn=978-0062862976 |language=en}}</ref>  He worked as a [[cartoonist]] for the school newspaper, ''The Crusader'', in addition to being a class officer and editor of a science literary magazine.<ref name="biogInfo" /> He also won a [[President's Volunteer Service Award]] and, in 1986, was named the Fenwick Scholar, the college's highest academic honor.<ref name="biogInfo" /> He graduated from Holy Cross with a [[Bachelor of Arts]], ''[[summa cum laude]]'', in physics as valedictorian in 1987.<ref name="biogInfo" /> As the Fenwick Scholar, he was granted exemption from classes to pursue research as a senior and completed a thesis titled, "Functional Neuromuscular Stimulation: An Analysis of the Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Foundations of Walking".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Past Fenwick Scholars, Projects and Advisors |url=https://hcappsdev.holycross.edu/hcs/hcweb/college-scholar-programs/fenwick-scholar-program/past-fenwick-scholars-projects-and-advisors.html |access-date=2023-12-19 |website=[[College of the Holy Cross]] |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":52" /> 

After graduating from Holy Cross, Collins was awarded a [[Rhodes Scholar]]ship to study in England at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Hopkin |first=Karen |date=May 1, 2008 |title=Switched on Science |url=https://www.the-scientist.com/switched-on-science-45191 |access-date=2024-08-17 |website=[[The Scientist (magazine)|The Scientist]] |language=en}}</ref> As a Rhodes Scholar, he earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (D.Phil.) in [[medical engineering]] from [[Balliol College, Oxford]], in 1990.<ref>{{Cite web |date=28 October 2020 |title=Dickson Prize in Medicine awarded to Balliol alumnus |url=https://www.balliol.ox.ac.uk/news/2020/october/dickson-prize-in-medicine-awarded-to-balliol-alumnus |access-date=2023-09-04 |website=[[Balliol College, Oxford]] |publisher=[[University of Oxford]] |language=en}}</ref> His doctoral dissertation, completed under John J. O'Connor at the [[Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford|Department of Engineering Science]], was titled, "Joint Mechanics: Modelling of the Lower Limb".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dissertations: Joint mechanics: modelling of the lower limb |url=https://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/permalink/44OXF_INST/35n82s/alma990110290180107026 |access-date=2023-12-19 |website=Oxford SOLO |publisher=[[Oxford Libraries Information System]] |language=en}}</ref> While pursuing his doctorate, he played as a member of the [[Oxford University Men's Basketball]] team and earned an [[Oxford Blue]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1989, while still a doctoral student, Collins began a collaboration with mathematician [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]], with whom he published a series of papers on animal locomotion during the 1990s.<ref name=":1" />

== Academic career ==

=== Boston University (1990–2014) ===
[[File:Jimcollins.jpg|thumb|Collins in 2009]]
After receiving his doctorate, Collins joined the faculty of [[Boston University]] (BU) in 1990.<ref name=":0" /> One of his early research focuses included [[kinesiology]]; he developed a series of devices to improve locomotion, neural function, and cardiac function, including vibrating insoles.<ref name=":0" /> He was appointed a professor of [[biomedical engineering]] at the [[Boston University College of Engineering]], where he co-founded the Center for BioDynamics in 1997 and served as its director,<ref name=":6" /> and earned multiple recognitions for teaching, including being named the college's "Biomedical Engineering Teacher of the Year" and the university's "Professor of the Year".<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=President Names First Warren Professors {{!}} BU Today |url=https://www.bu.edu/articles/2009/president-names-first-warren-professors/ |access-date=2026-05-25 |website=Boston University |language=en}}</ref> He won the university's Metcalf Cup and Prize for Excellence in Teaching in 2000, the university's highest teaching honor.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Brick |first=Tricia |date=Spring 2006 |title=Genius at Work |pages=20–25 |newspaper=Bostonia |url=http://www.bu.edu/bostonia/archives/2006/spring/collins/index.shtml |url-status=dead |access-date=June 12, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121019061512/http://www.bu.edu/bostonia/archives/2006/spring/collins/index.shtml |archive-date=October 19, 2012}}</ref> While at BU, he simultaneously taught at [[Harvard Medical School]] from 1998 to 2010.<ref name=":6" />  

In 1999, Collins, along with his biomedical engineering student Timothy Gardner, executed one of the first attempts to engineer genomes to perform certain functions. Together, they edited the genes of [[E. coli]] bacteria to create or stop creating certain proteins. Their findings of a genetic on/off, or "toggle switch," were published in [[Nature (journal)|''Nature'']] in an article now considered seminal in the field of synthetic biology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The New Transformers {{!}} The Brink |url=https://www.bu.edu/articles/2014/the-new-transformers/ |access-date=2026-05-28 |website=Boston University |language=en}}</ref> In October 2003, he became the first bioengineer to be awarded a [[MacArthur Fellowship]],<ref name=":4">{{Cite news |last=Tucker |first=Ian |date=2011-05-21 |title=James Collins: A spoonful of sugar helps the medicine go down |url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2011/may/22/my-bright-idea-james-collins |access-date=2024-04-22 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> which he received for "identifying abstract principles underlying complex biological phenomena such as motor control during standing and walking".<ref name="macarthur">{{cite web | title=MacArthur Fellows, October 2003 | publisher=John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation |url=http://www.macfound.org/site/c.lkLXJ8MQKrH/b.1142737/k.6839/Fellows_List__October_2003.htm | access-date=April 15, 2007 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071016151133/http://www.macfound.org/site/c.lkLXJ8MQKrH/b.1142737/k.6839/Fellows_List__October_2003.htm | archive-date=October 16, 2007 }}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=James J. Collins: Biomedical Engineer |url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/class-of-2003/james-j-collins |access-date=2026-05-25 |website=[[MacArthur Foundation]] |language=en|date=October 5, 2003}}</ref> That same year, he was the director of the Applied Biodynamics Laboratory at BU.<ref name=":5" /> In 2008, he was named a [[principal investigator]] of the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]]—the first from Boston University—to pursue research in [[gene expression]] and antibiotic resistance in single cells.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Frink |first=Kate |date=Fall 2008 |title=Collins Named BU's First HHMI Investigator |url=https://www.bu.edu/eng/files/2022/10/eng.alumni.2008-Fall-ENG-Magazine.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240708050031/https://www.bu.edu/eng/files/2022/10/eng.alumni.2008-Fall-ENG-Magazine.pdf |archive-date=2024-07-08 |access-date=2026-05-25 |website= |page=14}}</ref> On May 18, 2009, he was appointed as one of BU’s two inaugural William F. Warren Distinguished Professors, alongside [[George Annas]].<ref name=":3" /> In 2010, he was appointed by President [[Barack Obama]] to the [[Presidential Commission for the Study of Bioethical Issues]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jim J. Collins, Ph.D. {{!}} Catalio Capital Management |url=https://www.cataliocapital.com//team/jim-j-collins-ph-d,%20https://cataliocapital.com/team/jim-j-collins-ph-d |access-date=2023-12-19 |website=www.cataliocapital.com }}{{Dead link|date=October 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

By 2011, Collins held five appointments at Boston University: William F. Warren Distinguished Professor, University Professor, Professor of Biomedical Engineering, Professor of Medicine, and co-director of the Center for BioDynamics.<ref>{{Citation |last=Threats |first=Institute of Medicine (US) Forum on Microbial |title=Speaker Biographies |date=2011 |work=The Science and Applications of Synthetic and Systems Biology: Workshop Summary |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK84434/ |access-date=2026-05-25 |publisher=National Academies Press (US) |language=en}}</ref> That same year, he became the third BU professor to be elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]]; by that time, his research focused on the invention of synthetic gene networks and the development of techniques to improve biological function and devices to treat brain failure and other diseases, such as [[Parkinson's disease]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=ENG’s James Collins Honored for Research {{!}} BU Today |url=https://www.bu.edu/articles/2011/engs-james-collins-honored-for-research/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Boston University |language=en}}</ref>

=== Massachusetts Institute of Technology (2014–present) ===
{{Infobox laboratory
| name = Antibiotics-AI Project
| website = {{URL|https://www.collinslab.mit.edu/antibiotics-ai-project}}
}}In December 2014, Collins moved to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), where he was appointed the Termeer Professor of Medical Engineering & Science and was additionally named a professor at the [[Institute for Medical Engineering and Science]].<ref name=":0" /> Since then, he has been a joint professor in the MIT Department of Biological Engineering and a faculty member of the Biophysics Program, the Synthetic Biology Center, Microbiology Graduate Program, Computational & Systems Biology Initiative, and Center for Microbiome Informatics & Therapeutics, all at MIT.<ref name=":6" /> He has also been a visiting professor of engineering science at the [[University of Oxford]] since 2023.<ref name=":6" />
[[File:MIT Professor James J. Collins, GAEA Talks.png|thumb|272x272px|Collins in 2025]]
In 2016, Collins was appointed Allen Distinguished Investigator by the [[Allen Institute]] to research potential synthetic biology applications to antimicrobial resistance in [[drug-resistant bacteria]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-03-15 |title=James Collins named new Allen Distinguished Investigator |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/james-collins-named-new-allen-distinguished-investigator/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Wyss Institute |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Shaner |first=Karen |date=2016-04-13 |title=James Collins appointed 2016 Allen Distinguished Investigator |url=https://news.mit.edu/2016/collins-appointed-allen-distinguished-investigator-0413 |access-date=2023-12-19 |website=[[MIT News]] |publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] |language=en}}</ref> On October 3, 2018, he was named by [[Anantha Chandrakasan]], the dean of the [[MIT School of Engineering]], as faculty lead of the [[MIT Jameel Clinic|MIT Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health]], alongside [[Regina Barzilay]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 3, 2018 |title=Regina Barzilay, James Collins, and Phil Sharp join leadership of new effort on machine learning in health |url=https://news.mit.edu/2018/mit-barzilay-collins-sharp-lead-j-clinic-machine-learning-health-1003 |access-date=November 13, 2020 |website=[[MIT News]] |publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=People |url=https://www.jclinic.mit.edu/people |access-date=November 13, 2020 |website=J-Clinic |language=en |archive-date=November 30, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130200807/https://www.jclinic.mit.edu/people |url-status=dead }}</ref> In addition to the MIT Jameel Clinic, he leads the Antibiotics-AI Project at MIT, a research initiative which uses [[deep learning]] to discover new antibiotics.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Trafton |first=Anne |date=2023-12-20 |title=Using AI, MIT researchers identify a new class of antibiotic candidates |url=https://news.mit.edu/2023/using-ai-mit-researchers-identify-antibiotic-candidates-1220 |access-date=2024-05-06 |website=[[MIT News]] |publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] |language=en}}</ref> In 2024, he became a member of the [[Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research]].<ref name=":6" /> He is currently a member of the editorial board of the scientific journals [[Science (journal)|''Science'']], [[Cell (journal)|''Cell'']], and the [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|''Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences'']].<ref name=":6" />

Collins has been involved with a number of start-up companies, and his inventions and technologies have been licensed by over 25 biotech and medical device companies.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Saunders |first=Fenella |date=2023-02-06 |title=Synthesizing Engineering and Biology |url=https://www.americanscientist.org/article/synthesizing-engineering-and-biology |access-date=2023-12-19 |website=[[American Scientist]] |publisher=[[Sigma Xi]] |language=en}}</ref> He is the co-founder of the biomedical companies Senti Biosciences, Sherlock Biosciences, and Cellarity.<ref name=":6" />

=== Harvard University ===
Collins has been a visiting professor of systems biology at [[Harvard Medical School]] since 2008.<ref name=":6" /> That same year, he became a founding Core Faculty Member of the [[Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering]], where he currently is lead of Living Cellular Devices.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=2016-08-05 |title=Core Faculty: James J. Collins, Ph.D. |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/team/core-faculty/james-collins/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=[[Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering|Wyss Institute]] |language=en-US}}</ref> He has also been a member and senior associate<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-12-03 |title=Harvard’s Wyss Institute welcomes Massachusetts Institute of Technology as a new collaborating institution |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/harvards-wyss-institute-welcomes-massachusetts-institute-of-technology-as-a-new-collaborating-institution/ |access-date=2026-05-28 |website=Wyss Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> of the [[Broad Institute]] of Harvard and MIT and a professor of the [[Harvard–MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology]] since 2014.<ref name=":6" /> 

== Research ==

=== Synthetic biology ===
{{external media|video1=[https://www.ted.com/talks/jim_collins_how_we_re_using_ai_to_discover_new_antibiotics How we're using AI to discover new antibiotics], TedX (2020)|width=210px|float=right|headerimage=|video2=[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HB906zshzDw&t=105s James Collins: Doing Good Science with an Underdog Spirit], Harvard Biotech (2026)|video3=}}
Collins' work on synthetic gene circuits launched the field of [[synthetic biology]].<ref name="nature_editorial">[http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v463/n7279/full/463269b.html Editorial:  Ten years of synergy], Nature 463, 269-270 (21 January 2010),  doi:10.1038/463269b</ref>  He was the first (along with [[Michael Elowitz]] and [[Stanislas Leibler]]) to show that one can harness the biophysical properties of nucleic acids and proteins to create biological circuits, which can be used to rewire and reprogram living cells.

In a paper published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'',<ref name="toggle">{{cite journal | last=Gardner | first=TS |author2=Cantor CR |author3=Collins JJ | date=January 20, 2000 | title=Construction of a genetic toggle switch in Escherichia coli
 | journal=Nature | volume=403 | pages=339–342 | pmid=10659857 | doi=10.1038/35002131 | issue=6767| bibcode=2000Natur.403..339G | s2cid=345059 }}</ref> Collins designed and constructed a genetic toggle switch – a synthetic, bistable gene regulatory network – in E. coli.  The toggle switch forms a synthetic, addressable cellular memory unit with broad implications for biophysics, biomedicine and biotechnology. In the same issue of Nature, Elowitz and Leibler showed that one can build a synthetic genetic oscillator (called the repressilator) in E. coli.<ref name="pmid10659856">{{cite journal| author=Elowitz MB, Leibler S| title=A synthetic oscillatory network of transcriptional regulators. | journal=Nature | year= 2000 | volume= 403 | issue= 6767 | pages= 335–8 | pmid=10659856 | doi=10.1038/35002125 | pmc= | bibcode=2000Natur.403..335E | s2cid=41632754 }}</ref> Collins’ Nature paper on the genetic toggle switch<ref name="toggle" /> and Elowitz's and Leibler's Nature paper<ref name="pmid10659856" /> on the repressilator are considered landmark pieces which began the field of synthetic biology.<ref name="nature_editorial" />

Building on this work, Collins showed that synthetic gene networks can be used as regulatory modules and interfaced with a microbe's genetic circuitry to create programmable cells for a variety applications,<ref name="pmid15159530">{{cite journal| author=Kobayashi H, Kaern M, Araki M, Chung K, Gardner TS, Cantor CR | display-authors=etal| title=Programmable cells: interfacing natural and engineered gene networks. | journal=Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | year= 2004 | volume= 101 | issue= 22 | pages= 8414–9 | pmid=15159530 | doi=10.1073/pnas.0402940101 | pmc=420408 | bibcode=2004PNAS..101.8414K| doi-access=free}}</ref> e.g., synthetic probiotics to serve as living diagnostics and living therapeutics to detect, treat and prevent infections such as cholera and C. difficile.<ref name="pmid29899022">{{cite journal| author=Mao N, Cubillos-Ruiz A, Cameron DE, Collins JJ| title=Probiotic strains detect and suppress cholera in mice. | journal=Sci Transl Med | year= 2018 | volume= 10 | issue= 445 | article-number=eaao2586 | pmid=29899022 | doi=10.1126/scitranslmed.aao2586 | pmc=7821980 }}</ref><ref name="pmid35411114">{{cite journal| author=Cubillos-Ruiz A, Alcantar MA, Donghia NM, Cárdenas P, Avila-Pacheco J, Collins JJ| title=An engineered live biotherapeutic for the prevention of antibiotic-induced dysbiosis. | journal=Nat Biomed Eng | year= 2022 | volume= 6 | issue= 7 | pages= 910–921 | pmid=35411114 | doi=10.1038/s41551-022-00871-9 | pmc= | s2cid=248100868 | hdl=1721.1/147989 | hdl-access=free }}</ref> He also designed and constructed engineered riboregulators (RNA switches) for sensing and control,<ref name="PMID 15208640">{{cite journal | author =  Isaacs, FJ | title =  Engineered riboregulators enable post-transcriptional control of gene expression | journal = Nat Biotechnol | volume = 22 | issue = 7 |  pages = 823–4 2004 | year = 2004 | pmid = 15208640 | last2 =  Dwyer | first2 =  DJ | last3 =  Ding | first3 =  C | last4 =  Pervouchine | first4 =  DD | last5 =  Cantor | first5 =  CR | last6 =  Collins | first6 = JJ | doi = 10.1038/nbt986| s2cid = 7289450 }}</ref><ref name="pmid25417166">{{cite journal| author=Green AA, Silver PA, Collins JJ, Yin P| title=Toehold switches: de-novo-designed regulators of gene expression. | journal=Cell | year= 2014 | volume= 159 | issue= 4 | pages= 925–39 | pmid=25417166 | doi=10.1016/j.cell.2014.10.002 | pmc=4265554 }}</ref><ref name="pmid28746304">{{cite journal| author=Green AA, Kim J, Ma D, Silver PA, Collins JJ, Yin P| title=Complex cellular logic computation using ribocomputing devices. | journal=Nature | year= 2017 | volume= 548 | issue= 7665 | pages= 117–121 | pmid=28746304 | doi=10.1038/nature23271 | pmc=6078203 | bibcode=2017Natur.548..117G }}</ref><ref name="pmid33028812">{{cite journal| author=Angenent-Mari NM, Garruss AS, Soenksen LR, Church G, Collins JJ| title=A deep learning approach to programmable RNA In the context of synthetic biology and regenerative medicine, Collins collaborated with [[Derrick Rossi]] and [[George Q. Daley]] on a study using synthetic mRNA technology for biomedical applications. The team showed that synthetic mRNA could be used for highly efficient stem cell reprogramming and redifferentiation. This work was published in Cell Stem Cell in 2010,<ref name="pmid20888316">{{cite journal| author=Warren L, Manos PD, Ahfeldt T, Loh YH, Li H, Lau F | display-authors=etal| title=Highly efficient reprogramming to pluripotency and directed differentiation of human cells with synthetic modified mRNA. | journal=Cell Stem Cell | year= 2010 | volume= 7 | issue= 5 | pages= 618–30 | pmid=20888316 | doi=10.1016/j.stem.2010.08.012 | pmc=3656821 }}</ref> and Rossi used this synthetic biology technology platform to found [[Moderna]].<ref name="ekx">{{cite news |last1=Kutz |first1=Erin |title=ModeRNA, Stealth Startup Backed By Flagship, Unveils New Way to Make Stem Cells |url=https://xconomy.com/boston/2010/10/04/moderna-stealth-startup-backed-by-flagship-unveils-new-way-to-make-stem-cells/ |publisher=Xconomy, Inc |date=4 October 2010 |archive-date=February 8, 2017 |access-date=April 1, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170208132839/http://www.xconomy.com/boston/2010/10/04/moderna-stealth-startup-backed-by-flagship-unveils-new-way-to-make-stem-cells/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Collins has also used synthetic biology approaches (computational and experimental) to identify and address significant biological physics questions regarding the regulation of gene expression and cell dynamics. Collins, for example, has utilized synthetic gene networks to study the effects of positive feedback in genetic modules,<ref name="pmid10681449">{{cite journal| author=Hasty J, Pradines J, Dolnik M, Collins JJ| title=Noise-based switches and amplifiers for gene expression. | journal=Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | year= 2000 | volume= 97 | issue= 5 | pages= 2075–80 | pmid=10681449 | doi=10.1073/pnas.1332628100 | pmc=164653 | bibcode=2003PNAS..100.7714I | doi-access=free }}</ref> the role and origin of stochastic fluctuations in eukaryotic gene expression,<ref === Antibiotics and antibiotic resistance ===

Collins is also one of the leading researchers in systems biology through the use of experimental-computational biophysical techniques to reverse engineer and analyze endogenous gene regulatory networks.<ref name="pmid11983907">{{cite journal| author=Yeung MK, Tegnér J, Collins JJ| title=Reverse engineering gene networks using singular value decomposition and robust regression. | journal=Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | year= 2002 | volume= 99 | issue= 9 | pages= 6163–8 | pmid=11983907 | doi=10.1073/pnas.092576199 | pmc=122920 | bibcode=2002PNAS...99.6163Y | doi-access=free }}</ref>  Collins and collaborators showed that reverse-engineered gene networks can be used to identify drug targets, biological mediators and disease biomarkers.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Gardner | first=TS |author2=di Bernardo D |author3=Lorenz D |author4=Collins JJ | date=July 4, 2003 | title=Inferring genetic networks and identifying compound of action via expression profiling
 | journal=Science | volume=301 | pages=102–105 | pmid=12843395 | doi=10.1126/science.1081900 | issue=5629| s2cid=8356492 }}</ref>

Collins and collaborators discovered, using systems biology approaches, that all classes of bactericidal antibiotics induce a common oxidative damage cellular death pathway.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/j.cell.2007.06.049 | last=Kohanski | first=MA |author2=Dwyer DJ |author3=Hayete B |author4=Lawrence CA |author5=Collins JJ. | year=2007 | title=A common mechanism of cellular death induced by bactericidal antibiotics. | journal=Cell | volume=130 | issue=5 | pages=797–810 | pmid=17803904| s2cid=1103795 | doi-access=free }}</ref> This finding indicates that targeting bacterials systems that remediate oxidative damage, including the SOS DNA damage response, is a viable means of enhancing the effectiveness of all major classes of antibiotics and limiting the emergence of antibiotic resistance. This work established a mechanistic relationship between bacterial metabolism and antibiotic efficacy, which was further developed and validated by Collins and his team in a series of follow-on studies.<ref name="pmid19013277">{{cite journal| author=Kohanski MA, Dwyer DJ, Wierzbowski J, Cottarel G, Collins JJ| title=Mistranslation of membrane proteins and two-component system activation trigger antibiotic-mediated cell death. | journal=Cell | year= 2008 | volume= 135 | issue= 4 | pages= 679–90 | pmid=19013277 | doi=10.1016/j.cell.2008.09.038 | pmc=2684502 }}</ref>

Collins showed that certain metabolites could be used to enable bactericidal antibiotics to eradicate persistent, tolerant infections.<ref name="pmid21562562">{{cite journal| author=Allison KR, Brynildsen MP, Collins JJ| title=Metabolite-enabled eradication of bacterial persisters by aminoglycosides. | journal=Nature | year= 2011 | volume= 473 | issue= 7346 | pages= 216–20 | pmid=21562562 | doi=10.1038/nature10069 | pmc=3145328 | bibcode=2011Natur.473..216A }}</ref> Additionally, Collins and co-workers discovered that sublethal levels of antibiotics activate mutagenesis by stimulating the production of reactive oxygen species, leading to multidrug resistance.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2010.01.003 | last=Kohanski | first=MA |author2=DePristo MA |author3=Collins JJ. | year=2010 | title=Sublethal antibiotic treatment leads to multidrug resistance via radical-induced mutagenesis. | journal=Molecular Cell | volume=37 | issue=3 | pages=311–320 | pmid=20159551 | pmc=2840266}}</ref> Collins and colleagues, using their systems approaches, also discovered a population-based resistance mechanism constituting a form of kin selection whereby a small number of resistant bacterial mutants, in the face of antibiotic stress, can, at some cost to themselves, provide protection to other more vulnerable, cells, enhancing the survival capacity of the overall population in stressful environments.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1038/nature09354 | last=Lee | first=HH |author2=Molla MN |author3=Cantor CR |author4=Collins JJ. | year=2010 | title=Bacterial charity work leads to population-wide resistance. | journal=Nature | volume=467 | issue=7311 | pages=82–85 | pmid=20811456 | pmc=2936489| bibcode=2010Natur.467...82L }}</ref>

In 2020, Collins was part of the team—with fellow MIT Jameel Clinic faculty lead Professor [[Regina Barzilay]]—that announced the discovery through [[deep learning]] of [[halicin]], the first new [[antibiotic]] compound for 30 years, which kills over 35 powerful [[bacteria]], including [[Antimicrobial resistance|antimicrobial-resistant]] [[tuberculosis]], the superbug [[Clostridioides difficile (bacteria)|''C. difficile'']], and two of the [[World Health Organization]]'s top-three most deadly bacteria.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stokes|first1=Jonathan M.|last2=Yang|first2=Kevin|last3=Swanson|first3=Kyle|last4=Jin|first4=Wengong|last5=Cubillos-Ruiz|first5=Andres|last6=Donghia|first6=Nina M.|last7=MacNair|first7=Craig R.|last8=French|first8=Shawn|last9=Carfrae|first9=Lindsey A.|last10=Bloom-Ackermann|first10=Zohar|last11=Tran|first11=Victoria M.|date=February 20, 2020|title=A Deep Learning Approach to Antibiotic Discovery|journal=Cell|volume=180|issue=4|pages=688–702.e13|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2020.01.021| pmc=8349178|issn=1097-4172|pmid=32084340|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 2020, Collins, Barzilay and the MIT Jameel Clinic were also awarded funding through [[The Audacious Project]] to create the Antibiotics-AI Project<ref>{{Cite web|title=Collins Lab Antibiotics-AI Project|url=https://collinslab.mit.edu/antibiotics-ai-project}}</ref> and expand on the discovery of halicin in using AI to respond to the antibiotic resistance crisis through the development of new classes of antibiotics.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Jim Collins receives funding to harness AI for drug discovery|url=https://news.mit.edu/2020/jim-collins-receives-funding-harness-ai-drug-discovery-0422|access-date=November 13, 2020|website=MIT News {{!}} Massachusetts Institute of Technology|date=April 23, 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Nonlinear dynamics in biological systems ===

Collins also pioneered the development and use of nonlinear dynamical approaches to study, mimic and improve biological function,<ref name="pmid10057531">{{cite journal| author=Collins JJ| title=Random walking during quiet standing. | journal=Phys Rev Lett | year= 1994 | volume= 73 | issue= 5 | pages= 764–767 | pmid=10057531 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.73.764 | pmc= | bibcode=1994PhRvL..73..764C }}</ref> expanding our ability to understand and harness the physics of living systems. Collins, for example, proposed that input noise could be used to enhance sensory function and motor control in humans.<ref name="pmid7617033">{{cite journal| author=Collins JJ, Chow CC, Imhoff TT| title=Stochastic resonance without tuning. | journal=Nature | year= 1995 | volume= 376 | issue= 6537 | pages= 236–8 | pmid=7617033 | doi=10.1038/376236a0 | pmc= | bibcode=1995Natur.376..236C | s2cid=4314968 }}</ref><ref name="pmid8836253">{{cite journal| author=Collins JJ, Imhoff TT, Grigg P| title=Noise-enhanced information transmission in rat SA1 cutaneous mechanoreceptors via aperiodic stochastic resonance. | journal=J Neurophysiol | year= 1996 | volume= 76 | issue= 1 | pages= 642–5 | pmid=8836253 | doi=10.1152/jn.1996.76.1.642 | pmc= }}</ref>  He and collaborators showed that touch sensation and balance control in young and older adults, patients with stroke, and patients with diabetic neuropathy could be improved with the application of sub-sensory mechanical noise,<ref name="pmid8893000">{{cite journal| author=Collins JJ, Imhoff TT, Grigg P| title=Noise-enhanced tactile sensation. | journal=Nature | year= 1996 | volume= 383 | issue= 6603 | pages= 770 | pmid=8893000 | doi=10.1038/383770a0 | pmc= | bibcode=1996Natur.383..770C | s2cid=3660648 | doi-access=free }}</ref> e.g., via vibrating insoles.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Priplata | first=A |author2=Niemi J |author3=Harry J |author4=Lipsitz LA |author5=Collins JJ
 | date=October 4, 2003 | title=Vibrating insoles and balance control in elderly people
 | journal=The Lancet | volume=362 | issue=9390 | pages=1123–1124
 | pmid=14550702 | doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(03)14470-4| s2cid=33216209 }}</ref> This work has led to the creation of a new class of medical devices to address complications resulting from diabetic neuropathy, restore brain function following stroke, and improve elderly balance.

== Awards and honors ==
Collins' scientific accomplishments have been recognized by numerous awards. In addition to receiving a [[MacArthur Genius|MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship]] in 2003,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2003-12-01 |title=Five in Physics Are 2003 MacArthur Fellows |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/news/five-in-physics-are-2003-macarthur-fellows |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=PHYSICS TODAY |language=en}}</ref> he was named one of the top 50 science and technology leaders of 2005 by ''[[Scientific American]]'', for "Designing Artificial Life".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scientific American 50: SA 50 Winners and Contributors |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/scientific-american-50-sa/ |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Collins makes Scientific American list of science and tech leaders {{!}} BU Today |url=https://www.bu.edu/articles/2005/collins-makes-scientific-american-list-of-science-and-tech-leaders/ |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=Boston University |language=en}}</ref> He had also been named as one of 100 young innovators shaping the future of technology in the [[Innovators Under 35]] by ''[[MIT Technology Review]]'' in 1999.<ref name="tr100">{{cite web |date=November–December 1999 |title=1999 Young Innovator, James Collins |url=http://www.technologyreview.com/tr35/Profile.aspx?Cand=T&TRID=498 |access-date=April 15, 2007 |publisher=Technology Review}}</ref> In 2007, he was awarded the [[National Institutes of Health Director's Pioneer Award]] for his project "A Network Biology Approach to Antibiotic Action and Bacterial Defense Mechanisms",<ref>{{Cite web |title=Funded Research |url=https://commonfund.nih.gov/pioneer/fundedresearch |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=commonfund.nih.gov}}</ref> for which he received $25 million in funding over five years.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Faculty Awards {{!}} BU Today |url=https://www.bu.edu/articles/2008/faculty-awards/ |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=Boston University |language=en}}</ref> That same year, he was named a Senior Scholar Awardee in Aging Research by the [[Ellison Medical Foundation]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=EMF News: Senior Scholar Awardees in Aging for 2007 |url=http://www.ellisonfoundation.org/news_detail.jsp?id=105 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070917060924/http://www.ellisonfoundation.org/news_detail.jsp?id=105 |archive-date=2007-09-17 |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=www.ellisonfoundation.org}}</ref> In 2010, he won the [[Lagrange Prize|Lagrange-CRT Foundation Prize]], given by the [[Institute for Scientific Interchange]], for "outstanding contributions relevant to the progress of complexity science".<ref>{{Cite web |title=James Collins Wins Lagrange Prize {{!}} BU Today |url=https://www.bu.edu/articles/2010/james-collins-wins-lagrange-prize/ |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=Boston University |language=en}}</ref> 

Collins is an elected member of all three U.S. national academies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=James J. Collins, PhD |url=https://be.mit.edu/faculty/james-j-collins/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=MIT Department of Biological Engineering |publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1999, he was elected a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in biological physics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Fellows archive: James Collins |url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/aps-fellowship?q=James%20Joseph%20Collins&af=true |access-date=May 27, 2026 |publisher=[[American Physical Society]]}}</ref> In 2000, he was elected a fellow of the [[American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Foreign Member: James Collins |url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Collins_James |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=[[Academia Europaea]]|date=2026}}</ref> In 2002, he was elected a fellow of the [[Institute of Physics]] in the United Kingdom.<ref name=":6" /> In 2011, he was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] for his contributions to synthetic biology and genetic engineering.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-02-09 |title=James J. Collins Elected a Member of the National Academy of Engineering |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/james-j-collins-elected-a-member-of-the-national-academy-of-engineering/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Wyss Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> In 2012, he was elected a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in the area of Mathematical and Physical Sciences.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-04-23 |title=James Joseph Collins {{!}} American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/james-joseph-collins |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=www.amacad.org |language=en}}</ref> Collins was formally inducted into the academy on October 6, 2012.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-04-19 |title=Jim Collins to be inducted to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/jim-collins-to-be-inducted-to-the-american-academy-of-arts-and-sciences/ |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=Wyss Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> On October 15, 2012, he was elected to the [[National Academy of Medicine]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=ENG’s Collins Elected to Institute of Medicine {{!}} BU Today |url=https://www.bu.edu/articles/2012/james-collins-elected-to-institute-of-medicine/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Boston University |language=en}}</ref> In 2014, he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=BU’s James Collins Elected to National Academy of Sciences {{!}} The Brink |url=https://www.bu.edu/articles/2014/bus-james-collins-elected-to-national-academy-of-sciences/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Boston University |language=en}}</ref> in the areas of Engineering Sciences, Biophysics, and Computational Biology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=James J. Collins |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/james-j-collins-yjanml/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=National Academy of Sciences |language=en-US}}</ref> On November 25, 2013, he was elected a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in the field of Engineering.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AAAS Council Elects 388 New AAAS Fellows {{!}} American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) |url=https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-council-elects-388-new-aaas-fellows |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260518194847/https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-council-elects-388-new-aaas-fellows |archive-date=2026-05-18 |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2013-11-26 |title=Two Wyss Faculty Named AAAS Fellows |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/two-wyss-faculty-named-aaas-fellows/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Wyss Institute |language=en-US}}</ref>   

On November 13, 2012, Collins, together with [[Peter Palese]], [[Jeffrey V. Ravetch|Jeffrey Ravetch]], and [[John Mekalanos]], received the Sanofi-Institut Pasteur Award in [[Paris]], France, for "reducing antibiotic resistance and establishing innovative new treatments for bacterial infections".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-02-03 |title=The Award Winners 2012 |url=https://www.pasteur.fr/fr/nous-soutenir/comment-nous-soutenir/entreprises-fondations/ils-nous-soutiennent/sanofi-institut-pasteur-awards/award-winners-2012?language=fr |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Institut Pasteur |language=fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-11-14 |title=Collins wins eminent Sanofi-Institut Pasteur Award |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/collins-wins-eminent-sanofi-institut-pasteur-award/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Wyss Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> In September 2014, he was awarded the [[Human Frontier Science Program]] (HFSP)'s [[HFSP Nakasone Award|Nakasone Award]] for innovating synthetic gene networks and programmable cells.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-09-08 |title=Wyss Institute Core Faculty James Collins to receive the Human Frontier Science Program Nakasone Award |url=https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/faculty-member-awarded-for-innovation/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Wyss Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> He received the [[Robert A. Pritzker Distinguished Lecture Award]] that same year.<ref name=":6" /> On October 18, 2017, he was awarded the Jacob and Louise Gabbay Award in Biotechnology and Medicine at [[Brandeis University]] "for his inventive work in synthetic biology that created a new area of research, enabling multiple biomedical applications and launching a new sector of the biotechnology industry".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gabbay Award Winners |url=https://www.brandeis.edu/rosenstiel/gabbay-award/past.html |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=www.brandeis.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Collins won the 2020 [[Max Delbruck Prize|Max Delbruck Prize in Biological Physics]], conferred by the [[American Physical Society]], for "pioneering contributions at the interface of physics and biology, in particular the establishment of the field of synthetic biology and applications of statistical physics and nonlinear dynamics in biology and medicine".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-09-26 |title=Professor James Collins wins 2020 Max Delbruck Prize in Biological Physics |url=https://imes.mit.edu/news-events/professor-james-collins-wins-2020-max-delbruck-prize-biological-physics |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Institute for Medical Engineering & Science |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=admin |date=2019-10-24 |title=American Physical Society honors three MIT professors for physics research |url=https://physics.mit.edu/news/american-physical-society-honors-three-mit-professors-for-physics-research/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=MIT Physics |language=en-US}}</ref> That same year, he was awarded the [[Dickson Prize in Medicine]], the highest honor of the [[University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine]], for pioneering synthetic biology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Request Rejected |url=https://www.dicksonprize.pitt.edu/recipients/2020-collins.php |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=www.dicksonprize.pitt.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-11-09 |title=James Collins is awarded the 2020 Dickson Prize for Medicine for pioneering research |url=https://imes.mit.edu/news-events/james-collins-awarded-2020-dickson-prize-medicine-pioneering-research |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Institute for Medical Engineering & Science |language=en}}</ref> In 2021, he was awarded the [[Marvin J. Johnson Award|Marvin J. Johnson Award in Microbial and Biochemical Technology]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=BIOT Awards {{!}} The Marvin J. Johnson Award in Microbial and Biochemical Technology |url=https://acsbiot.org/biot-awards-the-marvin-j-johnson-award-in-microbial-and-biochemical-technology/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=ACS BIOT |language=en-US}}</ref> He was also awarded the 2021 Sigma Xi Walston Chubb Award for Innovation, which honors scientific and engineering creativity.<ref>{{Cite web |title=James J. Collins |url=https://www.sigmaxi.org/programs/prizes-awards/william-procter/award-winner/james-j.-collins |access-date=2026-05-28 |website=www.sigmaxi.org}}</ref> In 2023, Collins was named a [[Clarivate Citation Laureates|Clarivate Citation Laureate]] along with [[Michael Elowitz]] and [[Stanislas Leibler]] "for pioneering work on synthetic gene circuits, which launched the field of synthetic biology",<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-09-22 |title=James J. Collins named a Citation Laureate |url=https://hst.mit.edu/news-events/james-j-collins-named-citation-laureate |access-date=2023-12-19 |website=Harvard-MIT Health Sciences and Technology |language=en}}</ref> and was awarded the [[Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology]] for his same work on gene circuits.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-27 |title=Feynman Prizes Winners 2023 |url=https://foresight.org/press/feynman-prizes-winners-2023/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Foresight Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> He received the [[IET Achievement Medal]] that same year.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 23, 2023 |title=World leading engineers win at IET Achievement Awards |url=https://www.theiet.org/media/press-releases/press-releases-2023/press-releases-2023-october-december/23-october-2023-world-leading-engineers-win-at-iet-achievement-awards |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=www.theiet.org}}</ref> 

In 2025, Collins was awarded the [[IEEE Medal for Innovations in Healthcare Technology]] for "contributions to synthetic gene circuits and programmable cells, launching the field of synthetic biology, impacting healthcare applications".<ref>{{Cite news |title=James J. Collins {{!}} IEEE Awards |url=https://corporate-awards.ieee.org/recipient/james-j-collins/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251024024707/https://corporate-awards.ieee.org/recipient/james-j-collins/ |archive-date=2025-10-24 |access-date=2026-05-25 |work=IEEE Awards |language=en-US}}</ref> In 2026, he was awarded the Tel Aviv University International Prize in Biophysics for "pioneering contributions to quantitative and synthetic biophysics".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-05-07 |title=MIT School of Engineering faculty receive awards in winter 2026 |url=https://news.mit.edu/2026/school-engineering-faculty-receive-awards-0507 |access-date=2026-05-28 |website=MIT News {{!}} Massachusetts Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Silva |first=Jordan |date=2026-05-07 |title=MIT School of Engineering faculty receive awards in winter 2026 |url=https://news.mit.edu/2026/school-engineering-faculty-receive-awards-0507 |access-date=2026-05-28 |website=[[MIT News]] |language=en}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Collins married Mary McNaughton, a classmate at the [[College of the Holy Cross]], in 1990.<ref name="biogInfo" /> She is a professor at [[Harvard Medical School]] and a physician at [[Massachusetts General Hospital]].<ref name="biogInfo" /> They have two children: Katie, a [[Marshall Scholar]] at the [[University of Cambridge]], and Danny, a [[Knight-Hennessy Scholars|Knight-Hennessy Scholar]] at [[Stanford University]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=2022-10-05 |title=Healthcare and Life Sciences: James Collins |url=https://www.irishamerica.com/honoree/james-t-collins/ |access-date=2023-12-19 |website=Irish America |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2023-10-19|title=Duke Senior Launches Himself Towards Big Regwards|url=https://https/|access-date=2024-09-29|website=Duke Today|language=en-US|archive-date=June 25, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200625000000/https://https//udn.com/news/story/121424/4659358|url-status=dead}}</ref>
